analysis.one_liner: Wipes out a rule requiring mortgage lenders to disclose more detail about their home loans.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would erase expanded public disclosure of mortgage lending data, drew no cosponsors and died in the House Financial Services Committee without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would nullify a 2015 Consumer Financial Protection Bureau rule that expanded what home mortgage lenders must publicly report, including details about loan pricing, borrower characteristics, and where loans are and are not made [S2][S3]. That data is what regulators, researchers, and community groups use to spot discriminatory lending and neighborhoods being redlined. The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in the Financial Services Committee until the Congress ended [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Mortgage lenders and banks, who would be spared the cost of collecting and reporting the expanded loan data, and would face less public scrutiny of where and on what terms they lend [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: The bill declares that the CFPB's 2015 Home Mortgage Disclosure (Regulation C) rule has no force or effect, erasing the expanded reporting obligations it imposed on financial institutions [S3].
The 2015 rule expanded the scope of information financial institutions must disclose about home mortgages, so nullifying it removes those added disclosure requirements [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary borrowers and the communities they live in would lose the detailed public data that shows who is getting mortgages, at what cost, and which neighborhoods lenders are avoiding — the same data regulators use to enforce fair-lending laws [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: The expanded disclosures were designed to make mortgage lending more transparent; nullifying them would cut off the public record used to detect discrimination in who gets loans and on what terms [S2][S3].
The bill does not replace the rule with anything; it simply erases it, leaving lenders with fewer reporting obligations and the public with less information about access to home credit [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — lower compliance paperwork for lenders — comes entirely at the cost of transparency into mortgage markets. The disclosed data underpins fair-lending enforcement and public research on whether neighborhoods and demographic groups have equal access to home loans; erasing it without any substitute favors lenders over borrowers and communities.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, never got a hearing or a vote, and expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Andy Biggs introduced the bill on January 9, 2023, and it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services [S5].
The bill attracted no cosponsors over the two-year Congress [S4].
Its only actions were introduction and referral to committee; no markup, hearing, or floor vote ever occurred, and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mortgage lenders gained nothing — but they lost nothing either, since the 2015 disclosure rule remains in effect. The public retains the expanded mortgage lending data the bill would have erased.

for.name: Rep. Andy Biggs
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to nullify the CFPB's expanded mortgage disclosure rule; it drew no cosponsors [S1][S4][S5].

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, markup, or vote — letting it die when the Congress ended [S5].

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Republican sponsor, zero cosponsors from either party, and no vote ever occurred, so no partisan split is measurable [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would have freed lenders from the expanded 2015 HMDA reporting obligations, reducing compliance costs. Its failure means lenders remain subject to those disclosures, which expose lending patterns to fair-lending enforcement and public scrutiny [S2][S3].
The bill was a direct nullification of one of the bureau's signature rules. Its death leaves the CFPB's expanded mortgage data regime intact [S2][S3].
